analysis.one_liner: Gives Americans legal rights over their personal data and restricts how companies collect and sell it.
analysis.headline: A bipartisan House committee approved the bill 53 to 2 in July 2022, but House leaders never scheduled a floor vote before the Congress ended in January 2023, so the bill died.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would set a national privacy baseline: companies could only collect data reasonably needed to provide the service you asked for, and they could not sell or hand off sensitive data without your clear, affirmative consent. You would gain rights to see, correct, delete, and take your data with you, plus a way to opt out of targeted advertising, and companies could not use your data to discriminate against you. Children and teens would get extra protections, including a ban on targeted ads to anyone under 17. The FTC and state attorneys general would enforce the rules, and individuals could sue violators starting two years after enactment.
analysis.who_benefits: Everyone who uses the internet or apps: you get enforceable rights to access, correct, and delete the data companies hold on you, to opt out of data sales and targeted advertising, and to know where your data goes. Kids and teens get the strongest protections, including a ban on targeted advertising to minors under 17. The FTC, state attorneys general, and eventually individuals themselves could enforce the rules.

how_it_helps.text: Companies could only collect, process, or transfer personal data that is reasonably necessary to provide the product or service you requested, plus a short list of specified purposes.

Companies generally could not transfer sensitive data — health, location, biometric, genetic, financial, and private communications — without your affirmative express consent, and silence or continued use of a service would not count as consent.
Individuals would gain rights to access, correct, delete, and export their data, and could opt out of data transfers to third parties and out of targeted advertising.
The bill bans targeted advertising to anyone under 17, restricts transfers of minors' data without parental or minor consent, and creates an FTC Youth Privacy and Marketing Division.
Companies could not use personal data to discriminate based on protected characteristics, and could not punish you for exercising your privacy rights by raising prices or degrading service.
The FTC and state attorneys general would enforce the law, and individuals could sue violators in court starting two years after enactment.

analysis.who_pays: Companies whose business depends on collecting, processing, and selling personal data: data brokers, ad-tech firms, and large platforms would face compliance costs, restrictions on data sales, opt-out obligations, registration requirements, and FTC enforcement, cutting into the revenue their data practices generate.
analysis.who_pays_short: Data brokers, ad-tech, and large platforms

drawbacks.text: The bill preempts state privacy laws in the areas it covers, except for carve-outs for California, Illinois, and certain categories of state laws — meaning it would freeze or limit the ability of other states to adopt stronger protections in the future.

Individuals' right to sue violators would not begin until two years after enactment (the original version said four years), and would be subject to notification requirements, so people harmed by violations would have no direct remedy in the meantime.

Compliance would cost businesses of every size real money — new privacy policies, request-handling systems, security programs, and in some cases FTC rulemaking-driven changes — costs that could be passed to consumers even though small businesses get lighter timelines and protections.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core rights — data minimization, consent for sensitive-data transfers, deletion rights, and protections for minors — would meaningfully constrain a data industry that currently faces no comprehensive federal privacy law, and polling-free as the sources are, the committee's 53-2 bipartisan vote shows broad agreement the protections were worth having. The real tradeoffs are preemption, which locks in a national floor and could block stronger state laws later, and a two-year delay before individuals can sue. On balance the bill would have shifted power over personal data from companies to individuals, at real but manageable compliance cost.

outcome.mechanism: The House Energy and Commerce Committee approved it 53-2 and formally reported it to the House floor at the end of December 2022, but no floor vote ever came, and the bill expired when the Congress ended on January 3, 2023.

narrative.text: Representative Frank Pallone (D-NJ), chair of the Energy and Commerce Committee, introduced the bill on June 21, 2022 with an unusual bipartisan team: the committee's top Republican, Cathy McMorris Rodgers (R-WA), plus Democrats Jan Schakowsky (IL) and Gus Bilirakis (FL).
The bill moved fast in committee: a subcommittee forwarded it on a voice vote on June 23, and the full committee ordered it reported on July 20, 2022 by a vote of 53 to 2.
The committee's three cosponsors were two Republicans and one Democrat.
The committee formally reported the amended bill on December 30, 2022, placing it on the Union Calendar — the list of bills awaiting House floor action.
No House floor vote ever occurred, and the bill died when the 117th Congress ended on January 3, 2023.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Companies that profit from collecting, processing, and selling Americans' personal data — data brokers, ad-tech firms, and large platforms — keep operating under the same rules as before, facing no comprehensive federal privacy law. Consumers also lose the state-law patchwork question for now, since no national baseline replaced it.

sides.party_line_note: The bill was co-introduced by the committee's Democratic chair and top Republican, drew cosponsors from both parties (2 R, 1 D), and cleared committee 53-2 with members of both parties in favor; the obstacle was not a floor vote's outcome but that no vote was ever scheduled.

industries.note: Third-party collecting entities would face registration requirements, and companies would need consent before transferring sensitive data and must honor opt-outs of data transfers and targeted advertising — cutting directly into the revenue from reselling people's information.

industries.industry: Large social media platforms and big tech
industries.note: Platforms over $3 billion in revenue and 300 million users face special 'high-impact' duties, large data holders face short-form notices, metrics reporting, and executive responsibility requirements, and targeted ads to minors would be banned — threatening the data-driven advertising model.

The bill would for the first time place phone and broadband companies squarely under FTC privacy authority as covered entities, restricting their collection and transfer of customer data, though they are not the bill's primary target.

Section 209 provides small business protections and longer compliance timelines (90 days versus 45 for large data holders to respond to rights requests), softening the cost burden while still applying core privacy duties.
